text: Welcome back. This lesson covers the three tools you'll reach for constantly when operating Linux servers: grep to search text, sed to rewrite it, and awk to pull specific columns out of it. Together, piped into each other, they turn a raw log file or config file into exactly the information you need.

grep searches its input for lines matching a pattern and prints just those lines. Running it against nginx's error log on a Northbridge Retail web server instantly surfaces every connection failure and timeout, without you having to read through thousands of unrelated lines by hand.

A handful of flags make grep far more useful. -i ignores case, -v inverts the match to show lines that don't match, -r searches every file in a directory recursively, and -c just counts matching lines instead of printing them. Searching Northbridge's codebase recursively for TODO comments uses exactly that -r flag.

sed rewrites text using the substitute command — s, followed by a pattern, a replacement, and slashes separating the pieces. Run without -i it just prints the changed result; adding -i edits the file in place, which is how Northbridge's ops team flips a config setting from staging to production in one single command.

awk splits each line into fields by whitespace, or by any separator you specify with -F, and lets you print individual fields by number, like dollar-sign-one for the first column. Piping an access log through awk, sort, and uniq with a count is the fastest way to find which IP address is hitting the site hardest.

grep finds the lines you need, sed rewrites them, and awk extracts fields from them, and all three are built to pipe together. Up next, lesson sixteen: find and xargs, for locating files across a server and running a command against every single one you find.
